FrMS88-de3723-d1e111.summary: Poses the tenth question: whether being is said by the same formal notion of all creatures. Argument for: John 1, 'All things were made through him'; 'all' is a distributive sign, and only univocal terms can be distributed, so this would not be true unless being were univocal.
claims: Only univocal terms can be distributed, so 'all things' implies univocal being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e140.summary: Contrary: in the same place, 'without him was made nothing'.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e143.summary: Lays out four inquiries: whether being is said univocally of real being and being of reason (in and outside the soul), of absolute and respective, of substance and accident, and of being in potency and in act. Distinguishes being in the soul as what is wholly caused by the soul and as what is produced by the soul only in cognized being. First conclusion: being is not univocal to being in the soul (first sense) and outside the soul, since it is said of the latter simply and of the former only secundum quid, and univocal first-mode predication is simply, not secundum quid.
claims: Being in the soul can mean what is wholly caused by the soul or what is produced only in cognized being.
Being is not univocal to being wholly caused by the soul and being outside the soul.
Univocal predication in the first mode is simply, not secundum quid.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e187.summary: Second argument: the notion of being cannot be said of what includes incompossibles, but many beings of reason, such as fictions, do.
claims: Beings of reason such as fictions include incompossibles.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e197.summary: Third argument: being cannot be said univocally of being and its contradictory opposite, and being of reason is the contradictory of being, since nothing is a being of reason.
claims: Being of reason is the contradictory of real being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e206.summary: Fourth argument: no common univocal concept can be abstracted from contradictory extremes taken formally, else there would be a middle between contradictories. Then raises four objections, the first: many are certain that relation or number is a being while doubting whether it is real or of reason, so being is univocal to these.
claims: No univocal concept can be abstracted from formal contradictories.
Objection: certainty that relation is a being, with doubt whether real or of reason, implies univocity.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e228.summary: Second objection: things counted in something are univocal in it, and real being and being of reason are counted as several beings.
claims: Objection: real being and being of reason are counted as beings.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e241.summary: Third objection: a distributive sign seems to be added only to a univocal term, and 'every being is intelligible' distributes being over real being and being of reason.
claims: Objection: being is distributed over real and rational being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e250.summary: Fourth objection: the division of being into in the soul and outside the soul is not merely a division of a word into its significates, being by immediates, so it is a division of a univocal.
claims: Objection: the division into in and outside the soul is a division of a univocal.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e257.summary: Confirms the conclusion despite these: the common notion predicable of both would be either real (so something real predicated in quid of a being of reason) or made by the intellect (so a being of reason predicated in quid of real being), or a middle that is neither, which is impossible.
claims: No notion can be common in quid to real being and being of reason.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e278.summary: Reply to the first objection: such people are certain of a word, not of any thing or single formal notion.
claims: Certainty about the word 'being' does not entail a single formal notion.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e283.summary: Reply to the second: they are not properly counted, except as different acceptations of 'being', as a true man and a painted man are 'two men' only as two acceptations. To the others: it is not properly a division nor properly a distribution when speaking of being of reason.
claims: Real being and being of reason are counted only as different acceptations of 'being'.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e296.summary: Raises a difficulty: the first complex principle seems saved only where the formal notion of its subject extends, but it is saved in all beings of reason, so its subject extends to them.
claims: Objection: the first principle holds of beings of reason, so its subject (being) extends to them.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e307.summary: Reply: the first principle is saved in beings of reason in the same way its subject extends to them — only secundum quid and diminutively, as the notion of animal is saved in a painted animal.
claims: The first principle applies to beings of reason only diminutively.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e318.summary: Second conclusion: taking being in the soul in the second sense, as produced only in cognized being, being is said univocally of being outside and inside the soul.
claims: Being is univocal to the thing outside the soul and the thing as cognized.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e327.summary: First proof: when a determination added to a term does not diminish its formal quidditative notion, the same notion remains; being cognized does not diminish the formal notion of what is known, else knowing could annihilate everything, even what God made.
claims: Being cognized does not diminish the formal notion of what is known.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e341.summary: Second proof: no relation destroys its foundation but only posits its formal effect in it; cognized being is a relation of reason in the object, so it does not destroy the object's formal notion.
claims: Esse cognitum is a relation of reason in the object that leaves its foundation intact.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e350.summary: Third proof: what is numerically the same is the same in species and formal notion; what is in the thing is numerically the same as what is cognized.
claims: The thing in reality and the thing cognized are numerically the same.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e361.summary: Fourth proof: passing from potency to act never varies a thing's formal notion, and a thing potentially intelligible is brought to act by the act of understanding.
claims: Being actually understood does not vary a thing's formal notion.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e370.summary: Confirmation: either the act of understanding terminates at the external thing — and since terminating it is just receiving cognized being, they are the same in notion — or it terminates only at the species, and nothing of the thing is understood. Then begins four objections, the first: causes of different notions cannot have all the same effects; divine and human power differ in notion; so what God produces in real being could not be known by us, since knowing is producing in cognized being — which is false, so being in and outside the soul differ in notion.
claims: The act of understanding terminates at the external thing, giving it cognized being.
Objection: since divine and human powers differ, what is produced in real and in cognized being must differ in notion.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e407.summary: Second objection: whatever is produced in cognized being is known; in abstractive cognition only the species is produced; so only the species is known, which is false, or else the species, differing in notion from the object, shows the conclusion.
claims: Objection: in abstractive cognition only the species is produced.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e420.summary: Third objection: in intuitive cognition only the act of understanding is produced, so only it is known, and it differs entirely in notion from the external object.
claims: Objection: in intuitive cognition only the act is produced.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e432.summary: Fourth objection: by Meyronnes' own first conclusion, nothing is common to being simply and diminished being; real being is being simply, cognized being is secundum quid.
claims: Objection: cognized being is being secundum quid and shares nothing with real being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e441.summary: Reply to the first: two causes of different notions cannot have entirely the same effects as to being simply, but one may produce simple being and the other being secundum quid, as God produced the moon's being while the sun continually produces its being luminous.
claims: Different causes can produce the same thing in different respects, one simply and one secundum quid.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e457.summary: Reply to the second: in abstractive cognition, although only the act or species is produced in simple being, as regards cognized being the quiddity, not the species, is produced; to be known is to be produced in the second way.
claims: In abstractive cognition the quiddity is produced in cognized being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e466.summary: Reply to the third: in intuitive cognition something other than the act is produced, namely cognized being, which is formally in the object and produced by the act; so cognized being is not the act, which is produced only in real being.
claims: In intuitive cognition, cognized being is produced formally in the object, distinct from the act.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e477.summary: Reply to the fourth: there are two kinds of being secundum quid — one that diminishes the notion of what is determined (the subject of the earlier negative conclusion) and one that does not diminish but 'leaves aside'; cognized being is of the latter kind, not positing existence ('it is known, so it is' does not follow) yet not diminishing the formal notion.
claims: Cognized being is a secundum quid that leaves aside existence without diminishing the formal notion.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e493.summary: Alternatively, cognized being taken formally is perhaps only a being of reason and diminished, but taken fundamentally, for the substrate or object, it is the same quiddity as in the thing. Then gives the principal conclusion on the second doubt: being is said by the same notion of absolute and respective.
claims: Cognized being taken fundamentally is the same quiddity as in the thing.
Being is univocal to absolute and respective.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e512.summary: Proves it chiefly by the fundamental argument: the intellect cannot be certain and doubtful of the same under the same notion; it is certain that divine paternity is a being while doubting whether it is absolute or respective.
claims: Certainty that paternity is a being, with doubt whether absolute or respective, shows univocity.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e528.summary: Difficulty: then there would be some thing neither in itself nor toward another, which is a contradiction.
claims: Objection: a being neither ad se nor ad aliud is contradictory.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e533.summary: Reply: for things dividing something common, however immediate, there is no middle notion but only a notion abstracting from both, as number is either even or odd, with no number neither, yet the formal notion of number abstracts from both; similarly animal from rational and irrational.
claims: A common notion abstracts from immediate dividing differences without being a third thing.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e551.summary: Objection: everything is either ad se or not ad se, as contradictories; being, abstracting from both, is not ad se; whatever is not ad se is ad aliud; so being is ad aliud.
claims: Objection: what abstracts from ad se is not ad se, hence ad aliud.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e560.summary: Reply: when contradictory predicates are applied to immediate contraries, they must be distinguished: 'not ad se' is said of the respective in one way and of the common divided term in another. Then gives the third principal conclusion: being is said by the same formal notion of substance and accident, by the same arguments, especially the certain-and-doubtful concept argument.
claims: Contradictory predicates apply differently to a contrary and to the common term divided by contraries.
Being is univocal to substance and accident.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e584.summary: Difficulty: when the whole entity of one thing is in attribution to another, being is not said of them by the same notion; substance and accident are such.
claims: Objection: accidents exist wholly by attribution to substance, so being is not univocal.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e596.summary: Reply: the argument proves the opposite: when the whole entity of one is by attribution to another, being is said of them by the same formal notion.
claims: Attribution of accident to substance presupposes a common notion of being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e612.summary: Proves the major from Augustine (De Trinitate V): whatever is said relatively is something in itself; so what is something in attribution to another is something in itself, and hence formally a being. Then introduces the fourth principal question: whether being is said univocally of being in potency and in act.
claims: Whatever is relative is also something in itself, and hence formally a being.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e625.summary: Distinguishes subjective and objective potency; for subjective potency (matter) the earlier arguments suffice, and for objective potency, the harder case, affirms univocity.
claims: Being is univocal to being in objective potency and being in act.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e636.summary: First proof: act and potency do not diversify essence; the definition of man is the same in potency and in act.
claims: Act and potency do not diversify essence.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e643.summary: Second proof: dividing differences do not vary the formal notion of what is divided, and being is divided by potency and act.
claims: Being divided by potency and act keeps the same formal notion.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e648.summary: Third proof: what is numerically the same has the same formal notion; a grain or the like is numerically the same in potency and in act.
claims: A thing is numerically the same in potency and in act.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e658.summary: Fourth proof: an intrinsic mode does not vary the formal notion of what it modifies, since the quidditative notion abstracts from the mode; act and potency are intrinsic modes. First difficulty: whether the division of being into potency and act is quidditative; for subjective potency, no, since a quidditative division exhausts the divided and not everything is merely in subjective potency or in act; for objective potency and its opposite act, yes, since a quidditative division can extend to division by intrinsic modes — every quiddity is either in act or in potency.
claims: Act and objective potency are intrinsic modes not varying the formal notion.
The division of being by objective potency and act is quidditative; by subjective potency and act it is not.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e684.summary: Second difficulty: whether this is a formal division, i.e. one where a formal notion remains the same in both dividing members. Answers yes, since being is said by the same notion of being in act and in potency.
claims: The division of being into act and potency is a formal division.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e695.summary: Objection: what is said of one simply and of another secundum quid is not said by the same notion; being in act is being simply, but being in potency is not.
claims: Objection: being in potency is being only secundum quid.

FrMS88-de3723-d1e706.summary: Reply: grants the major but denies the minor, distinguishing 'is' as secundum adiacens (existence) and as tertium adiacens (copula with essential predicates). Being in potency is not simply being in the first sense, but in the second it is simply being and simply substance, as being in act is: 'a man in potency is simply a man' is true and 'a man in potency is a man secundum quid' false. The opening argument is answered by what has been said.
claims: Being in potency is not simply being existentially, but is simply being in the copulative sense.
'A man in potency is simply a man' is true.

FrMS88-de3723.summary: The tenth question of the prologue asks whether being is said by the same formal notion of all creatures, examining four pairs. (1) Real being and being in the soul: distinguishing being wholly caused by the soul (beings of reason, including fictions) from being produced by the soul only in cognized being (esse cognitum), Meyronnes denies univocity in the first case — being of reason is being only secundum quid, may include incompossibles, is the contradictory of real being, and no common notion could be either real or mind-made — answering that certainty about such items concerns only the word, and that the first principle applies to beings of reason only diminutively. In the second case he affirms univocity: cognized being does not diminish the formal notion of what is known, is a relation of reason that does not destroy its foundation, and is numerically the same as the thing; esse cognitum is a secundum quid that 'leaves aside' rather than 'diminishes', and the quiddity known is the same as the quiddity in the thing. (2) Absolute and respective: being is univocal, as shown by certainty that a divine person is a being while doubting whether it is absolute or respective; being abstracts from both without being a third thing, as number from even and odd. (3) Substance and accident: univocal, and the accident's attribution to substance actually confirms this, since (per Augustine) whatever is relative is also something in itself. (4) Being in potency and in act: with respect to objective potency, being is univocal, since act and potency are intrinsic modes not varying the essence; the division by objective potency and act is quidditative and formal; and being in potency is 'simply being' in the copulative (tertium adiacens) sense, though not existentially (secundum adiacens).
claims: Being is not univocal to real being and being wholly caused by the soul (beings of reason).
Being is univocal to the thing as real and the thing as cognized; esse cognitum does not diminish the formal notion of the thing.
Being is univocal to absolute and respective, abstracting from both as number from even and odd.
Being is univocal to substance and accident.
Being is univocal to being in objective potency and being in act, which are intrinsic modes.
Being in potency is simply being in the copulative sense but not in the existential sense.
